function.name: read
function.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

function.name: bash
function.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

function.name: edit
function.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

function.name: write
function.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

Done. The webapp is retrievable from the sample client.

## What was blocking

A single nonempty filter rule, scoped to the isolated sample network:

```
-A INPUT -i sample-server -p tcp -m tcp --dport 8080 -j DROP
```

This dropped the sample client's (10.77.0.2) connections to 10.77.0.1:8080. The webapp itself (`/opt/webapp.py`, pid 25) was healthy and listening the whole time — purely a firewall issue.

## Actions taken

1. **Backed up** the ruleset first → `/root/iptables-backup-20260917-221048.rules` (revertable with `iptables-restore`).
2. **`iptables -F`** — retired the nonempty filter rules; reasserted `-P INPUT/FORWARD/OUTPUT ACCEPT`.
3. Left the webapp process and `/testbed` files untouched (git is clean; no file changes were warranted).

## Verification

Per the runbook, tested from the independent local node rather than the host:

```
nsenter --net=/run/netns/sample-client -- curl --max-time 3 http://10.77.0.1:8080/
→ Public sample webapp: ready   (HTTP 200, 3/3 tries, <1ms)
```

All tables now empty with ACCEPT policies (`filter`, `nat`, `mangle`, `raw`, and `ip6tables`), confirmed via both `iptables -S` and `nft list ruleset`.

## Two things worth flagging

- **A host-local test gives a false pass.** `curl http://10.77.0.1:8080/` from the host returned HTTP 200 *even before* the flush, because locally-generated traffic doesn't traverse `-i sample-server`. Only the client-namespace test reflects the real client path — easy to be misled by here.
- **No persistence, so this fix is stable but also non-durable.** I checked for re-add mechanisms (no `cron`/`crontab`, no `systemd`/timers, no `/etc/iptables` or `/etc/sysconfig/iptables` rules file) and found none — nothing will re-apply the DROP rule. Conversely, since the ruleset isn't saved anywhere, a restart of this sample host comes up with empty ACCEPT chains, which matches the intended "only the public webapp exposed, no host firewall" state described in the runbook.

Scope note: I flushed the filter table as instructed, which is the only table that had rules. Given the host exposes just this one public example on an isolated sample network with no external connectivity, blanket ACCEPT policies are appropriate here; this approach would not be suitable for an internet-facing host.
